plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Downs cell, the industrial electrolytic apparatus used to produce pure sodium metal from molten sodium chloride via the reaction 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). The cell interior contains a bath of molten NaCl, with a cylindrical iron screen separating the electrode compartments; the cathode (−) occupies the outer annular region and the anode (+) projects upward from the bottom center, both connected to an external voltage source at the lower right. Liquid sodium metal, which is less dense than the molten salt, rises and collects in a side reservoir on the right, from which it drains through a labeled Na outlet; simultaneously, Cl2 gas produced at the anode rises through a central green-tinted collector tube and exits through a labeled Cl2 outlet at the upper right, while fresh NaCl is fed continuously through an inlet at the top. The iron screen physically segregates the two products — liquid sodium and gaseous chlorine — preventing their recombination and enabling continuous, separate collection of each. This figure demonstrates the Downs cell as the industrial-scale process for sodium production and explains why aqueous electrolysis cannot substitute for it, since H+ ions are more easily reduced than Na+ ions at any cathode in contact with water.

interactions.label: Run electrolysis
interactions.teaches: Na+ and Cl− ions move to opposite electrodes in molten salt, and the products leave by different physical paths: liquid sodium to the side reservoir and chlorine gas up the central outlet
Each electrode has a different half-reaction: Na+ gains electrons at the cathode to form sodium metal, while Cl− loses electrons at the anode to form chlorine gas

demo_steps.title: Identify the cell layout
demo_steps.narration: The Downs cell contains molten NaCl rather than water, with a central anode, an outer cathode region, and an iron screen separating the two product zones.

demo_steps.title: Follow ion migration
demo_steps.narration: When the animation runs, Cl− ions migrate toward the central anode while Na+ ions migrate toward the cathode compartment. This is the microscopic motion that drives the macroscopic production of chlorine and sodium.

demo_steps.title: Click the electrodes
demo_steps.narration: Click the cathode to see Na+ + e− → Na(l), then click the anode to see 2Cl− → Cl2(g) + 2e−. The signs of the electrodes determine which ion is reduced and which is oxidized.

demo_steps.title: Separate the products
demo_steps.narration: Chlorine gas rises through the central collector and exits through the Cl2 outlet, while less-dense liquid sodium collects in the side reservoir and drains through the Na outlet. The iron screen prevents the products from recombining.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The Downs cell works because molten salt supplies Na+ and Cl− without water, and the iron screen plus separate outlets keep newly formed sodium metal and chlorine gas apart.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original as a flat labeled cross-section: gray cell walls, pale blue-lavender molten NaCl bath, central tan anode, outer cathode compartment, curved black iron mesh screen around the center, green chlorine collector pipe rising upward and bending to the right, and pink-purple sodium reservoir on the right. Use arrows to emphasize product flow: chlorine upward and out the top, sodium into the right reservoir and out the side. During animation, show small blue Na+ particles drifting outward toward the cathode and small green-yellow Cl− particles drifting inward toward the anode; then show green Cl2 bubbles rising and pink sodium droplets collecting. Clicking either electrode should brighten that region and display its balanced half-reaction in a nearby callout without obscuring the apparatus labels.

authoredContext:
The most important method for the production of sodium is the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride; the set-up is a Downs cell , shown in . The reaction involved in this process is:

Separation of the molten sodium and chlorine prevents recombination. The liquid sodium, which is less dense than molten sodium chloride, floats to the surface and flows into a collector. The gaseous chlorine goes to storage tanks. Chlorine is also a valuable product.

Pure sodium metal is isolated by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride using a Downs cell. It is not possible to isolate sodium by electrolysis of aqueous solutions of sodium salts because hydrogen ions are more easily reduced than are sodium ions; as a result, hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead of the desired sodium metal. The high temperature required to melt NaCl means that liquid sodium metal forms.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram is a T-shaped structure labeled, “Anode ( positive sign ),” that is on a mesh-like background labeled, “Iron screen.” The anode is connected to a box labeled, “Voltage source,” by a line, and the voltage source is connected to one of two L-shaped structures that surround the anode. They are labeled, “Cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the cathode on the right side of the diagram is a tube connected to a collection chamber labeled, “N a metal,” that has a lower outlet labeled, “N a outlet.” Surrounding all of these components is a blue background labeled, “Molten N a C l,” and a series of tubes that form a square outside the diagram. They have an opening in the upper right corner labeled, “Inlet for N a C l.” At the top of the diagram is a large tube with an upward-facing arrow drawn on it. The tube turns right, has a right-facing arrow on it, and is labeled, “C l subscript 2 outlet.”
